summary: The bill expands HSA eligibility to anyone with any health coverage or in a health care sharing ministry, raises contribution limits to $10,800/$29,500, allows HSA funds to pay insurance premiums and periodic provider fees, treats sharing ministry payments as qualified expenses, and cuts the nonqualified withdrawal penalty to 10%.

scores.thoughts: The bill contains no provisions for direct government outlays or appropriations. All changes are to the tax code via expanded HSA tax advantages. This has no bearing on government spending levels.

The bill substantially expands HSA eligibility (removing the high-deductible requirement and allowing coverage under Medicare, Medicaid, etc.), dramatically raises contribution limits ($2,250 to $10,800 individual; $4,500 to $29,500 family), permits premium payments from HSAs, includes concierge-style fees and health care sharing ministry costs as qualified expenses, and lowers the nonqualified distribution penalty from 20% to 10%. These are all tax reductions via expanded deductions and exclusions.

The legislation is explicitly designed to broaden access to and use of HSAs as a market-based alternative to traditional insurance. It decouples HSAs from high-deductible plans, allows HSA funds for a wide array of private plans and direct-pay arrangements, and incorporates health care sharing ministries. This strongly advances private, consumer-directed healthcare over public or universal models.
No provisions relate to firearms, regulations, or Second Amendment issues.
No provisions address immigration, visas, border policy, or related pathways.
No provisions address reproductive health services, abortion access, or funding restrictions.
No provisions affect military budgets, defense authorizations, or related spending.
No provisions relate to environmental regulations, climate policy, or energy standards.

While the bill extends HSA eligibility to Medicaid and CHIP enrollees, it does not alter eligibility, benefit levels, or funding for welfare programs themselves. The core focus remains tax-advantaged private accounts rather than expansion or contraction of safety-net entitlements.
No provisions address schools, school choice, federal education funding, or privatization.
No provisions address drug criminalization, decriminalization, enforcement, or legalization.
No provisions address sentencing, policing, rehabilitation, or criminal procedure.
No provisions address tariffs, trade agreements, or globalization.

By expanding tax exclusions and deductions through higher HSA limits and broader eligibility, the bill increases tax expenditures and thereby widens deficits. This runs counter to prioritizing debt reduction.
No provisions address legal protections, nondiscrimination rules, or benefits for LGBTQ+ individuals.
No provisions address foreign assistance, international aid, or related funding.
No provisions address voting access, election administration, or voter ID.
No provisions address data privacy, technology regulation, or surveillance.
No provisions address collective bargaining, union rights, or employer flexibility.

The bill repeatedly incorporates health care sharing ministries (typically faith-based organizations) into HSA eligibility, qualified expenses, and medical-care definitions, while explicitly stating they are not to be treated as insurance. This provides favorable tax treatment to religiously oriented arrangements, creating a modest tilt toward religious exemptions.

The bill expands HSA eligibility, dramatically raises contribution limits, broadens qualified expenses, and lowers the penalty on nonqualified distributions. These changes reduce federal tax revenue by enlarging tax-advantaged accounts and deductions, thereby increasing the budget deficit.
